beats.narration_text: Research Computing on Explorer and AICR. Requesting Access to Explorer. Why a login alone isn't enough, the two ways to get added to a sponsor's storage space, and how to check you're in.

shot.visual_intent: Film identity and short teaching description, visible immediately; Liam speaks playlist, title, summary

beats.narration_text: Bonjour. This is Liam, in for Bear. First, a correction. Getting on Explorer isn't just a form and your login. Either way, you need a sponsor, someone whose storage space you belong to. This lecture covers the rule, the two ways in, what the form's first screen looks like, and how to check that it worked.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A PI: the principal investigator, the faculty member who leads a project. A sponsor: the PI or staff member who owns a storage space. A storage space: a folder under slash projects that a group shares. A delegate: a member the sponsor lets add other people. A member: someone who can read, write and run in the project. And Duo: the second sign-in check.

beats.narration_text: Here's the rule that decides everything. A Northeastern login alone won't get you onto Explorer. Every user has to belong to a storage space that a sponsor owns.

beats.narration_text: The sponsor is a PI or a staff member, and the space is a folder under slash projects. Research groups get it free, up to thirty-five terabytes. If a sponsor has no space yet, they request one first.

beats.narration_text: Four roles. The PI owns the project, and can add members, guests and delegates. A delegate can add members. A member reads, writes and runs. A guest reads and runs, but can't write.

beats.narration_text: Two routes in. Route A: your sponsor or their delegate adds you. Route B: you submit the access form. Research Computing recommends every PI name a delegate, so route A never waits on one person.

beats.narration_text: Route A has two ways. The simpler one needs no terminal. In Open OnDemand, under Files, is an app called Managing slash projects. The sponsor picks the group, types the usernames, comma-separated with no spaces, and clicks Launch. A log shows what changed.

beats.narration_text: The other way is a command. First, s run gets the sponsor or a delegate onto a node in the short partition. Then the project command names the project and your username. Several people go in as a comma-separated list, and view members checks the result.

beats.narration_text: Then wait. Changes can take up to two hours to reach the whole cluster. And once you're added, start a fresh login session, because your groups are read when you log in.

beats.narration_text: Rejected at the door? Either you have no Explorer account yet, or the username is wrong. Try the user I D from the form, then your email prefix. If you changed your password minutes ago, wait a while. If you're sure, submit the form.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Explorer needs a place in a sponsor's storage space, not just a login. Your sponsor adds you with one command, or you submit the access form. Try the user I D from the form first, and your first login settles it. Check with who am I and groups, and if it fails, ask your sponsor.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: I'm a new user of Northeastern's Explorer cluster. My Northeastern username is [my username] and my sponsor is [sponsor's name]. Write the short message I send them. It must give my username and the exact command they or a delegate should run, project [project name] add members [my username], on a node in the short partition. Keep it to four sentences. Then check two things yourself. Does the message give your username and the project name? And once your sponsor replies, does groups list the project?
